chunks: Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Masrur (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn Buttah said: A number of our companions narrated to me, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa ibn 'Ubayd, who said: Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said to me:
"What would you say if you were told: Inform me, is Allah, the Mighty and High, a Thing or is He not a thing?"

I said to him: Allah, the Mighty and High, has established Himself as a Thing where He says: 'Say: What thing is the weightiest in testimony? Say: Allah is a witness between you and me.' So I say: He is a Thing unlike other things, for in negating 'thing-ness' from Him is His nullification and negation,
He said to me: You are truthful and correct,
Then al-Rida (peace be upon him) said to me: People have three schools of thought regarding Divine Unity: negation, anthropomorphism, and affirmation without anthropomorphism,

The school of negation is not permissible, and the school of anthropomorphism is not permissible because nothing resembles Allah, Blessed and Exalted be He. The path in the third way is affirmation without anthropomorphism.
Chapter: What has come regarding Vision
ai.seo_question: What are the three schools of thought regarding Divine Unity (Tawhid) according to Imam al-Rida?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies that Allah is a 'Thing' (Shay') but distinct from created entities, citing Surah Al-An'am 6:19 to establish His self-testimony. He delineates three theological approaches to Tawhid—negation (naft), anthropomorphism (tashbih), and affirmation without resemblance (ithbat bi-la tashbih)—identifying the latter as the orthodox Shia position that avoids the extremes of denying existence or attributing physical form.
